budget_rule: Max USD 100 per person per night. With five people that means a group total of about USD 500 per night, however it is split. In a hotel five people need 2-3 rooms, which quietly breaks the 'two sharing a double' maths: the fifth person is the expensive one. Every hotel below therefore carries rooms_for_5 (how the five actually fit) and group_night_usd (the real nightly total for all five), and pp_night_usd = group_night_usd / 5.
selection_priority: Design and architecture first, then value, then price. Where a generic-but-cheap option and a beautiful-but-dearer one both fit, the beautiful one is listed. This is also why the walled-city colonial houses with plunge pools are weighted heavily: split five ways they are the only way to get genuinely beautiful architecture in Cartagena in March under USD 100 per person.
beach_verdict: Pick ISLA BARU, and stay on the quiet south/southwest side rather than on the Playa Blanca day-tripper strip. BarU is the only one of the five options that gives a group of five a real four-night base instead of a logistics exercise. It is joined to the mainland by the Barbacoas bridge, so you reach it in about an hour by road and you can leave whenever you like; every other candidate locks you into fixed boat windows. That matters specifically in early March: the December-to-May trade winds blow hard over this coast, mornings are calm and afternoons get choppy, so the Rosario and San Bernardo crossings (45-60 min and 2h+ of open water respectively, with a mandatory 3-4pm return) are the ones you least want to be committed to four days running. From Baru you still get the good water, because the Rosario reefs are a 20-40 minute private-boat hop and you go in the morning when the sea is flat. Playa Blanca itself is genuinely overrun between roughly 11am and 4pm by day boats and vendors, but if you sleep on the island it empties at dusk and dawn and is yours. Barú also owns the four best non-beach things to do down there: the bioluminescent plankton lagoon at Manzanillo (a night activity, so only stayers get it), the Aviario Nacional, the mangrove channels for kayaking, and Cholón. Runner-up, and the honest alternative if water clarity is the single thing you care about: ISLA GRANDE in the Rosarios, but take two nights there, not four, and expect rustic-not-designed hotels, rocky entries and one boat a day. Rejected: Tierra Bomba (15 min away and great for a day, but the water is brackish and mediocre and it is not a four-night place), Santa Marta/Tayrona/Palomino (a flight or a 4-5h drive, and most Tayrona beaches are closed to swimming for current - it breaks the no-moving rule), Isla Mucura/San Bernardo (beautiful, arguably the best water of all, but 2h+ of open sea each way in the windiest month with almost no exit options). BUDGET REALITY FOR FIVE: this is where Barú gets uncomfortable. The genuinely beautiful design hotels (Las Islas, Sofitel Barú Calablanca) are USD 430-460 for one double, so roughly USD 215-230 per person before you have housed the fifth. Of the five hotels listed below only two come in under USD 100 per person once you pay for three rooms. On this island the villa is not the budget compromise, it is the right answer: a private-pool beach house split five ways beats every in-budget hotel on architecture AND on price, and it solves the fifth-person problem outright.

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias
stops.area_note: Stay inside the walls. El Centro is the postcard half (cathedral, Plaza Santo Domingo, the best restaurants) and the most expensive; San Diego is the same walled city but quieter, more residential and slightly cheaper - for five people with taste, San Diego is the sweet spot. Getsemaní is 10 minutes' walk outside the Clock Tower gate, scruffier, covered in murals, and where Celele, Alquímico, Bazurto Social Club and Café Havana are; rooms run roughly 20-30 percent under Centro for the same quality. THE FIVE-PERSON PROBLEM: Cartagena's walled-city boutiques are tiny - Casa del Coliseo has 12 rooms, Amarla has 8 - so five people needing three rooms is a real constraint, not a formality. Three rooms in these hotels also pushes you to about USD 90-110 per person, right at the ceiling. The colonial houses are the genuinely better answer for a group this size: a 3-5 bedroom casona with a plunge pool, a courtyard, 18-foot ceilings and daily housekeeping runs USD 450-600 for the whole house, which is USD 90-120 each for architecture no hotel in this price band can touch, plus you get a kitchen and somewhere to drink before dinner. If the group is deciding between a good-but-ordinary hotel room at USD 84pp and a colonial house at USD 100pp, take the house. HONEST WARNING ON PRICING: early March is peak high season (the block runs mid-January through March at roughly 1.5-2x low-season rates). USD 100pp is workable but not generous - it buys the strong second tier, not the famous ones. Out of reach entirely: Casa San Agustín around USD 673 a night, Casa Pestagua around USD 709, Sofitel Legend Santa Clara around USD 593, the new Four Seasons around USD 690 - all for ONE double. GOOD NEWS ON DATES: Semana Santa 2027 starts on Palm Sunday, 21 March, so an early-March trip sits clear of the Easter spike, which is the single most expensive week of the Colombian year on this coast. If the dates ever slip into the third week of March you are brushing it and prices jump again - hold the early-March window. Book 2-3 months out regardless; the small boutiques sell out for March.

activities.name: Walled-city orientation walk and sunset on the muralla
activities.what: Land, drop bags, then walk Centro to San Diego to Las Bóvedas and up onto the sea wall for sunset. Three ways to do the sunset drink: Café del Mar, literally built on top of the ramparts, iconic and packed - reserve or arrive by 16:30, premium prices; Baluarte de Santo Domingo next door, much less crowded and noticeably cheaper; or Townhouse rooftop in San Diego, two wading pools and a sunset DJ, pool access around 50,000 COP. If you want the 360-degree view over old city, bay and skyline rather than just the sea, the Movich rooftop one block off Plaza Bolívar beats all of them - open to the public but it closes for private events, so call ahead.
activities.when: Day 1, 16:00 onwards (sunset roughly 18:10 in early March)

activities.name: First dinner: La Cevichería
activities.what: The Bourdain ceviche place on Calle Stuart by Plaza San Diego. Small and courtyard-ish, historically no reservations, so go at 18:30 or expect to queue - and a queue of five is worse than a queue of two. If it is brutal, El Boliche Cebichería a few streets away is the locals' better-value answer at $12-21.

activities.name: Bazurto market food tour
activities.what: Not the tourist version of Cartagena: the real wholesale market east of the centre, with a guide, eating through fruit stalls, fried-food stands, butchers and a sit-down lunch. Cartagena Connections and Juan Ballena both run it, typically a 10:30 start with local bus transport, fruit tasting and lunch included. Five is a good size - most operators cap small-group at six. Go with an operator, not alone.

activities.name: Castillo San Felipe de Barajas, late afternoon
activities.what: The big hilltop fortress with the tunnel network. Go at 16:00-17:30, not midday - there is no shade and March sun is punishing. About an hour and a half including the tunnels and the view back over the old city.

activities.name: Celele, then champeta at Bazurto Social Club
activities.what: Celele in Getsemaní is the reason food people fly here - No.5 in Latin America's 50 Best 2025, No.48 in the World's 50 Best, Caribbean-Colombian cooking out of the Caribe Project research. Mains $16-23, tasting around $78. Reservations are effectively mandatory: they lock the door after check-in, require a card and a minimum spend, and you need a week ahead on weekdays, two weeks for a weekend - and a table for five is harder than a table for two, so book the moment dates are fixed. Afterwards walk five minutes to Bazurto Social Club on Avenida del Centenario for live champeta and picó sound-system culture: the Palenque/Afro-Caribbean side of this city that the walled city hides.

activities.name: Getsemaní street-art and culture walk
activities.what: Two to three hours through the murals, Calle de la Sierpe, Plaza de la Trinidad and the Callejón Angosto umbrellas, with the gentrification and Afro-Caribbean history that goes with them. The shared graffiti walk is about $15-40; a private guide for the five of you with a snack runs nearer $40-60pp and is worth it. Morning, before the heat.

activities.name: Volcán del Totumo mud volcano (optional - judge it honestly)
activities.what: A 15-metre mud cone about an hour north where you climb in and float in warm grey clay, then rinse in the lagoon. Group half-day tours $35-45pp, small-group or private $50-65, or $5-6 at the gate if you drive yourselves. Worth knowing before you commit: it is kitschy and crowded, and the 'massage', 'photo help' and 'wash' each carry a $2 tip expectation that stacks up. Skip it if the group would rather do a proper Caribbean cooking class ($70-90pp) - same morning slot, better memory.

activities.name: Sunset sail on the bay, then chiva or Alquímico
activities.what: A shared sunset catamaran across Cartagena bay, 90 minutes to two hours, $25-50pp, usually with an open bar of rum drinks; Sibarita Express is the commonly recommended one. A private evening charter for just the five of you runs $500-750, i.e. $100-150pp - only worth it if you want the boat to yourselves. Then choose your night: the chiva rumbera painted party bus with a brass band and an aguardiente open bar (about $25-40pp, 3 hours, deliberately ridiculous), or the grown-up version - Alquímico on Calle del Colegio, three floors, herb-infused bottles glowing on two-storey shelves, a World's 50 Best Bars regular - then salsa at Café Havana in Getsemaní.

food.name: Celele
food.what: Colombian Caribbean, Latin America's 50 Best No.5, Getsemaní. Mains $16-23, tasting around $78. Book 1-2 weeks ahead; a card and a minimum spend are required, and a five-top needs more notice.

food.name: Carmen
food.what: Caribbean ingredients, European technique, El Centro. Mains $18-27, tasting $68-83. The other fine-dining anchor alongside Celele.

food.name: Marea by Rausch
food.what: Seafood and risotto on the Getsemaní waterfront by the Rausch brothers. $22-34 per person. The best of the smart-but-not-tasting-menu tier, and easier to seat five than Celele.

food.name: La Cevichería
food.what: The Bourdain ceviche house, Calle Stuart near Plaza San Diego, El Centro. $13-23. Go early, it queues.

food.name: La Cocina de Pepina
food.what: Proper costeño home cooking in Getsemaní - arroz de lisa, posta cartagenera. $9-15. The cheap meal you will actually talk about afterwards.

stops.weather_note: Early March is the dry season and about as good as this coast gets: lows around 24-25C, highs 30-32C, sea at 28-29C, roughly 11.6 hours of sun and very little rain. The catch is wind. December through May the trade winds blow steadily over the Caribbean coast and March sits inside that window - it keeps the city bearable and the mosquitoes down, but it also churns the sea. Mornings are calm; the water builds through the afternoon. That is why every boat activity in this plan is scheduled before noon. March is also firmly high season (mid-January to March, at roughly 1.5-2x low-season rates), so prices are at their annual peak. One piece of timing luck: Semana Santa 2027 opens on Palm Sunday, 21 March, so an early-March trip sits clear of the single most expensive week on this coast. Do not let the dates drift past mid-March.

stops.name: Isla Barú (south Barú / Playa Blanca)
stops.area_note: Barú is technically a peninsula, cut off by the Canal del Dique and reconnected by road in 2014, which is the whole point: you drive there in about an hour and you are not hostage to a boat schedule. Three distinct zones. (1) The Playa Blanca strip in the north - the famous white sand, and also the problem: day boats and vans dump crowds and vendors on it from roughly 11:00 to 16:00. Stay at the quiet end (Thani Ecobeach) and it empties completely at dusk. (2) The Cholón-facing west side - calmer water, the party-boat lagoon a short hop away, where Aura sits. (3) The south and southwest end past the Aviario - the best beaches, the fewest people, where Sabai, Casa Córdoba, Las Islas and Isla del Encanto are. For a design-conscious group wanting a scene without a party hostel, the south end is right, with one big private-boat day out to the Rosarios and Cholón. THE FIVE-PERSON PROBLEM IS WORSE HERE THAN IN CARTAGENA. Beach hotels charge per room and the rooms are expensive, so three rooms wrecks the maths: of the five hotels below only Thani and Aura come in under USD 100 per person. The postcard properties are hopeless for this budget - Las Islas is USD 460+ per double (USD 230pp for two, before the fifth person), Sofitel Barú Calablanca USD 430+, Isla del Encanto USD 338+. On the design-first rule the honest recommendation for Barú is therefore NOT a hotel: take a private-pool beach villa and split it five ways. A 4-bedroom beachfront house with its own pool comes out near USD 100pp, beats every in-budget hotel here on architecture, gives you a kitchen and a terrace, and removes the third-room penalty entirely. Also worth knowing: an oceanfront villa with its own dock means your charter boat collects you from the house rather than a public pier. Budget option if the group would rather spend on boats than beds: Soy Local Barú at around USD 108 a double on Playa Blanca (roughly USD 65pp across three rooms) - basic, not beautiful, but it frees up a lot of money.

activities.name: Transfer to Barú, then Playa Blanca after the day boats leave
activities.what: Private van from the walled city over the Barbacoas bridge, about 1h-1h15 door to door, roughly 350,000-450,000 COP (USD 85-110) for a van of five, so USD 17-22 each - have the hotel arrange it. Check in, then walk onto Playa Blanca around 16:30 once the day boats and vans have gone. This is the version of that beach worth seeing: same white sand, no vendors, no crowd, low light.

activities.name: Bioluminescent plankton night swim
activities.what: Small boat into the dark mangrove lagoon near Manzanillo del Mar / Portonaito, where the dinoflagellates flash blue when you move the water. This is the single best argument for sleeping on Barú rather than day-tripping it, because it only runs at night. Standalone from a Barú hotel, roughly $25-35pp; packaged as an evening excursion from Cartagena, $50-70pp. Go on the darkest night available - a bright moon washes it out completely, so check the moon phase against your dates before booking.

activities.name: Private boat charter: Rosario Islands, snorkelling and Cholón
activities.what: The big day, and the reason Barú works. Charter your own speedboat rather than joining a day tour: a 28ft (10-12 pax) runs from 1,800,000 COP, about USD 450, and a 29ft from about USD 475, captain and fuel included, cooler and sound system on board. Split five ways that is USD 90-95 each - better than the $93-125pp beach-club day passes and you control the route and the clock. Standard run: leave around 08:30 while the sea is still flat, snorkel the Rosario reefs (10-15m visibility, protected marine park), lunch at an island club, then Cholón in the afternoon - the anchored-boat lagoon where everyone rafts up, sound systems competing, floating bars selling ceviche and mojitos. Loud, messy, very Colombian, and far better on a boat you control. Add USD 7.50pp national park fee and USD 2pp maritime insurance, cash only.
activities.when: Day 5 - and take the first clear morning, never the afternoon

activities.name: Aviario Nacional de Colombia
activities.what: On Barú itself, so no boat: 21 exhibits across three reconstructed ecosystems, around 170 species, two daily flight demonstrations with a handler. Genuinely well done, and the best fallback for a blown-out windy morning. Foreign adult admission 90,000 COP (about USD 22) as of September 2026, students 65,000 COP.

activities.name: Kayak the mangrove channels, then nothing
activities.what: The lagoon side of Barú is threaded with mangrove channels you can paddle in flat water even when the open sea is blown out - which by mid-afternoon in March it often is. Several hotels lend the kit free: Thani Ecobeach includes a double kayak and a paddleboard at no charge. Then deliberately do nothing with the rest of the day. On a four-night beach stop, one empty day is the whole point.
activities.duration: 2 hours plus the rest of the day

activities.name: Morning snorkel, or a beach-club day pass
activities.what: Two ways to close it out. Either a half-day snorkel run to the Rosario coral gardens, roughly $40-70pp through your hotel - again, morning, when the water is clearest and calmest. Or take a day pass at one of the designed beach clubs and go horizontal: on Barú, Nena Beach Club, Sabai Beach Club, Mambo or Sunset Beach Club, and none charge a dock fee if you arrive by land. In the Rosarios, mid-range passes are $93-125pp including boat and lunch (Capri, Pa'ue, Mangata) - which is exactly why the private charter on day 5 is the better spend for five people.

activities.name: Last sunset, west-facing
activities.what: Barú faces west, so unlike Cartagena you get the sun dropping into open water straight off your own beach. No booking, no boat, no price. Back to Cartagena on day 8 by road, about an hour, and out.

food.name: Your hotel or villa
food.what: Be realistic: Barú is not a restaurant destination and most nights you eat where you sleep. Budget $15-30pp at Thani or Aura, more at Sabai. Thani's food is good but reviewers flag small portions for the price. A villa with a kitchen (and in some cases a cook) changes this equation considerably for five people.

food.name: Playa Manglares Isla Barú
food.what: The one property on the island with an actual food reputation - worth booking a table even if you sleep elsewhere. Roughly $25-40 per person.

food.name: Sabai Beach restaurant
food.what: Open to non-guests as well as guests, on the private beach at the southwest tip. The nicest setting for a long lunch on the island. $30-50 per person.

food.name: Nena Beach Club, Playa Blanca
food.what: Beach-club lunch on the famous sand: loungers, fried fish, coconut rice, cocktails. Usually a day pass or a minimum spend, roughly $30-50 per person.

food.name: Cholón floating vendors
food.what: Not a restaurant: boats that pull alongside yours in the lagoon selling ceviche, oysters and cocktails. Cash only, and agree the price out loud before anything is handed across. $10-20 per person.

stops.weather_note: Same dry-season numbers as Cartagena - 30-32C, sea at 28-29C, almost no rain - but on Barú the wind is not a footnote, it shapes the days. December to May the trade winds blow hard over this stretch and the practical effect is that mornings are glassy while afternoons get choppy, with local guides describing afternoon boat crossings in this season as genuinely challenging. Three consequences: book every boat activity for the morning; expect Playa Blanca's water to turn from turquoise to stirred-up and greenish on the windiest afternoons, sometimes with seaweed; and know that the wind masks the sun, so people burn badly here without noticing. The upside is real - it is the driest, clearest, least-mosquito time of year, with 11-plus hours of sun a day. Early March also sits clear of Semana Santa (Palm Sunday 21 March 2027), which on Barú means the difference between a quiet island and a Colombian domestic-holiday crush.

getting_around: GETTING THERE: as of 1 January 2027 Aerolíneas Argentinas flies Buenos Aires Aeroparque (AEP) to Cartagena nonstop, five times a week, so the trip opens and closes in Cartagena with no Bogotá connection and no domestic hop - which is precisely why a single beach base reachable by road is the right structure. Five times weekly means the return legs are fixed to specific days, so build the 3+4 nights around the flight days rather than the other way round. IN CARTAGENA: the walled city and Getsemaní are small and walkable - ten to fifteen minutes end to end, about ten minutes between the two through the Clock Tower gate. Taxis have no meters and no official tariff, so agree the fare out loud before getting in; short hops inside the centre run roughly 10,000-15,000 COP and the airport to the walled city is 15-20 minutes for about 25,000-35,000 COP. Uber, DiDi and InDriver all technically operate but driver coverage is thin and waits can be long; the simplest default at night is to have the hotel or restaurant call a taxi. Five people do not fit in one taxi - budget two cars for every trip, or book a van. A pre-booked private van transfer from the airport is worth it on arrival day. CARTAGENA TO BARU: by road over the Barbacoas bridge, an hour to an hour and fifteen; a private van for five costs roughly 350,000-450,000 COP (USD 85-110) each way, about USD 17-22 a head - have the Barú hotel or villa host arrange it, this is the standard way. By sea it is 45-60 minutes by speedboat and hotel transfers run about USD 35 per person each way, i.e. USD 175 for five, which is more than the van. Take the road: cheaper for a group, runs on your schedule, immune to the March wind. BOAT TRANSFERS GENERALLY: the Rosario Islands day-boat system from Muelle La Bodeguita near the Clock Tower is rigid - departures 07:50-08:30, mandatory return 15:00-16:00, 45-50 minutes of open water each way. Two government fees are collected in cash at the pier and cannot be paid by card: national park entrance 31,500 COP (about USD 7.50) and maritime insurance 8,800 COP (about USD 2). Some beach clubs instead leave from Marina Todomar in Bocagrande, so check the confirmation for which pier. Tierra Bomba water taxis are separate and cheap: 8,000 COP per person to Punta Arena from behind the hospital in Bocagrande, 10,000 COP to Bocachica from La Bodeguita, leaving when full rather than on a timetable. A private charter (USD 450-475 for a 28-29ft boat holding 10-12) removes all of this and, at USD 90-95 each for five, is the right call for the one big island day.
safety_note: Practical, not alarmist. The walled city, San Diego and Getsemaní are fine to walk day and evening and are visibly policed; violent crime against tourists is uncommon. After about midnight stick to the lit main streets in Getsemaní - the quiet side alleys empty out and that is where the opportunistic stuff happens. Normal city habits cover most of it: phone in your pocket not your hand, bag zipped and worn across the body in crowds, limited cash. Moving as a group of five is itself decent protection; splitting up at 2am is the thing that goes wrong. The real everyday risk here is not danger, it is the transactional street hustle. Agree the price out loud in pesos before accepting anything at all - a woven bracelet slipped onto your wrist, a flower pressed into your hand, oysters, a shoulder massage on the beach, a chair, or a photo with a palenquera (that is a paid transaction, roughly 10,000-20,000 COP, settle it before the camera comes up). Never accept a free sample; payment will be expected. Do not buy island tours from people selling them on the muralla or the beach - inflated prices, overcrowded boats, and the classic ruined day at Playa Blanca; book through your hotel or a known operator. In restaurants pick places with displayed prices and check the bill, noting that 'propina voluntaria' is genuinely voluntary. Agree taxi fares before getting in. Scopolamine drugging is rare but real, so watch your drink and take a taxi rather than walking long distances very late. On Barú: the public Playa Blanca strip has persistent vendors, and the boat channel has current, so swim in front of your hotel. And respect the March sun - the constant wind hides how badly you are burning.
